question: kit/07-QUALITY-BAR.md, R2, word for word
note: Each vote is one fresh agent that received one picture and the question of R2 and nothing else. The pictures carry neutral names; which judged frame each is stands in the key file, added when every answer is in.

votes.why: The repeated, lightly varied spider-like creatures read as copies of a single 3D asset scattered across the scene.

it looks like a well-lit but ordinary CG scene, probably a personal or stock render. The volumetric fog and lava glow are competent. But the walker creatures are simple and lack detail, the cracked ground texture repeats, and the cliffs are generic. It lacks the density and finish of a top-budget film or cinematic, and its lighting is too sophisticated for a web demo or mobile game.

The scene combines offline-style volumetric lighting and detailed foreground rock shaders with noticeably basic 3D assets and effects—especially the flat ground plane with thin uniform lava cracks, simplistic floating-debris fire patches, and a sharply bounded circular pit around the foreground creature—which points to an ordinary 3D render rather than a top-budget cinematic or a low-end real-time demo.
The distant mountains have conspicuously angular, sparsely faceted silhouettes characteristic of a low-budget real-time scene.

the image has film-quality atmospheric depth. Layered haze and smoke, glowing lava cracks, and detailed rock and ground textures all hold up at this scale, and the shot is composed like a cinematic still of an alien landscape with spindly creatures. Two things keep me from being more sure. The creatures are small and slightly stiff, and this could pass as a high-end artist render, which would make it (c).
The strongest cue is the lava's hard, uniformly glowing edge: it looks like an emissive material laid into textured terrain rather than convincingly lighting the surrounding rock.

the lava-field ground has stretched, smeared textures and the rocks are simple and blocky. Together with generic game-engine fog and lighting, that looks like an ordinary hobbyist or stock real-time render, not film-quality work. It could also be (d).

The low-poly foreground rocks and flat, sharp-edged lava plane that casts almost no emissive orange bounce light onto the surrounding ground, which is characteristic of a real-time web 3D demo, mobile game, or low-budget production rather than a high-end cinematic or offline render.
the foreground lava crust looks like a flat sheet covered with a stretched rock texture.

The main factor is the foreground. The lava-rock texture is stretched and smeared, and the rocks are simple, low-detail meshes. That points to a real-time game or indie scene, even though the haze, glowing lava and distant spider creatures are atmospheric. The runner-up is (b), at about 30.
The conspicuously repeated creature meshes across the terrain make it look like a conventional assembled 3D render.

the ground looks like a real-time game engine made it. It's a flat plane with tiled, repeating textures, the lighting is simple and the depth fog is uniform. The creatures look like copies of the same model (they resemble Morrowind silt striders, so it could be a fan remake or mod). It isn't polished enough for a big-budget cinematic, and it doesn't look like a typical stock render.
